analogy.name: A hospital triage desk
analogy.line: Test strategy is like hospital triage: assess who is most at risk, treat the serious cases first, run the right checks, keep monitoring, and decide openly who waits or goes home.

test-strategy.caption: You cannot test everything. Test the riskiest parts first, automate what repeats, and handle what is left deliberately.
steps: Triage starts by asking who is in danger. Risk assessment asks what would hurt most if it broke: the payment flow, or a settings page? Your answer decides where effort goes.
The sickest patients are seen first. Prioritise the riskiest areas for testing. High coverage of safe code is not the goal, and saying so shows judgement in an interview.
The right checks for each patient: boundary values, equivalence partitions and decision tables. Aim for one test per idea, not one per line of code.
Monitors run all the time. Automated tests run in CI on every change. A check that only runs by hand eventually does not run at all.
Some patients wait, some go home, a few are escalated, always by a named person. Defects are fixed, deferred or accepted on purpose. Ignored failures equal no tests.

analogy.name: A courier at a door
analogy.line: A UI test is like a courier: find the right door by its number (locator), wait until someone answers (auto-wait), deliver the parcel (act), check the signature (assert), and try once more if no one came.

selenium-playwright.caption: Flaky tests are usually timing, not bugs. Locate robustly, wait for ready, assert state, and retry once before trusting a failure.
steps: A courier follows the house number, not the colour of the door. A resilient locator uses a role, label or test id. Generated class names change and break the test.
The courier waits until someone opens, not for a fixed time. Auto-wait checks the element is ready. A fixed sleep is slow when things are fast and fails when slow.
Hand over the parcel only when the door is open. Playwright acts only when the element is visible and able to receive the click or typing, which removes a whole class of flakes.
Check the signature: assert what should now be true, such as text, URL or state. Assert behaviour a user sees, not internal implementation, so refactors do not break tests.
If no one answered, try once more. A single retry absorbs a one-off hiccup. If it still fails, the failure is real, so read it instead of rerunning until it goes green.

analogy.name: A signed agreement between neighbours
analogy.line: A contract test is like a written agreement between neighbours: the consumer states what it needs, the agreement is written down (pact), the provider proves it can keep it, and then both can renovate separately.

api-testing.caption: Contract tests let two teams deploy independently. The consumer writes what it expects, and the provider proves it can deliver it.
steps: The consumer is the neighbour stating what they need, in their own terms. Its tests define the exact request and response shape it relies on, no more.
The pact is the agreement on paper. It is a file both sides can read and neither can silently change, which makes expectations reviewable instead of tribal knowledge.
The provider is the other neighbour proving they can keep the deal. It replays the pact against the real service on every change, so breaking a consumer fails the build early.
Green means both can deploy apart. Consumer and provider ship without waiting for each other or running a slow shared environment. This is the pitch for contract tests.

analogy.name: Tuning a race car
analogy.line: Performance work is like tuning a race car: practise on the real circuit (model), do timed laps (run), read the telemetry (measure), then fix the slowest part and go again.

performance-testing.caption: Performance work is a loop: model the real workload, run it, measure where time goes, fix the slowest part, and run it again.
steps: Practise on the real circuit, not an empty car park. A realistic workload uses real paths, data shapes and concurrency. A fake workload measures a fake system.
Do timed laps while watching the whole car, not only the stopwatch. Drive the load and watch CPU, memory, database and queues, because the symptom is rarely where the cause is.
Telemetry tells you which part is slow. APM shows where time goes across services and queries. Guessing the bottleneck is how people optimise the wrong thing.
Fix the slowest part first, then do another lap. One bottleneck at a time, re-measured, shows the effect of each change and stops you chasing noise.

analogy.name: Securing a castle
analogy.line: Defense in depth is like a castle: inspect the plans (code), vet the suppliers (dependencies), test the gates with a mock attack (running app), and keep guards on the walls (runtime).

appsec.caption: No single check catches everything. Read the code, scan dependencies, probe the running app and watch production.
steps: Inspecting the plans is SAST: a scanner reads your source for patterns such as injection and unsafe calls. It runs early, before anything is deployed, but cannot see runtime behaviour.
Vetting suppliers is SCA: knowing which libraries you ship and which have known flaws. Most vulnerabilities arrive through a dependency, not code you wrote.
A mock attack on the gates is DAST: probing the live app from outside, as an attacker would. It finds what is exposed and misconfigured, but not why.
Guards on the walls are runtime monitoring in production. The earlier layers are predictions. Logs, alerts and anomaly detection tell you what is really happening.

analogy.name: Planning a house security review
analogy.line: Threat modeling is like securing a house: sketch the floor plan (data flow), mark which rooms are public and which private (trust boundary), then ask at each door how a burglar might get through (STRIDE).

threat-modeling.caption: Threat modeling starts with a drawing: who talks to what, and where trust changes. STRIDE comes after the drawing, never before.
steps: Sketch the floor plan: who talks to what, honestly and completely. No threats yet. A good picture of the system is what makes the later questions useful.
Mark which rooms are public and which are private. The trust boundary separates what you control from what you do not. The database sits deepest inside, so protect it most.
At each door in the boundary, ask STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege. Work one threat at a time.
